It was left to fired MI6 librarian Connie Sachs (played by actress Beryl Reid) to reveal the Russian deceptions involved then (just as they are in Tokyo today) in identifying hidden Russian spies, and how she succeeded in doing so. 

Smiley comes to Connie with a name, only a name, "Polyakov, Alexey Alexandrovich Polyakov. Cultural attache, Soviet embassy, London." Connie nods her head absently, and then starts in: "Born in the Ukraine. Married, but unaccompanied by wife." Here Connie paused, looked up directly into Smiley's eyes, and scowled angrily "And a six-cylinder Karla-trained hood if ever I saw one." (Karla being the notorious Russian spymaster always being sough by MI6.) For the rest of that scene, and for the rest of the story, please do spend the six hours needed to view all six parts of this BBC gem from the early 1980's.

Why of why does Russian espionage so frequently follow this exact same pattern of attempted deception? And here we all have thought all of these years that chess was really a Russian game.

Steven J. Herrup

That age questioned old certitudes of church and state and looked at them again under the light of reason. comments.name: John
comments.body:
Perhaps this would make a good movie script, but it seems a bit implausible.

A data center contains row upon row of servers, sort of like the warehouse at the end of "Raiders of the Lost Ark". Many of these servers are running  multiple VMs that store the data. Identifying the servers that need to be removed would be impossible without inside help.

As others have pointed out, large corporations replicate the data across multiple geographic regions because they cannot afford a single point of failure and any single datacenter can be taken offline by acts of nature or man.

I am pretty sure that most nations have a good idea where these datacenters exist within the confines of adversary nations. In this age of connected warfare, I imagine they are high up on the targeting list. Just a thought.

comments.name: Bruce Maier
comments.body:
As a life long IT/Computer professional, the data needs to be split up, not residing in a single location. This is the opposite of the overall trend in computing.

E.g. (1) Each centralized computer had it's own telephone/communications network. Now we have the Internet. (2) Each disk based data storage was managed by different, disparate software systems. Now we have DBMS, (3) We used to have separate telephone, cable TV, over the air TV channels, rented physical movie VCR tapes/DVD disks, now it all arrives over the single Internet connection to our home. (4) We used to have multiple computer vendors with their own, unique hardware and operating systems, now we have standard hardware and Windows or a Unix/Linux variant.

Data centers are the continuation of the trend. But consolidation also creates single points of failure. It is easier to manage and operate, and easier to disrupt.

(I started when computers were HUGE, and I was a teenager, in the late 1960s. I saw the hardware infrastructure of the predecessor of the Internet in the 1970s. It has been a ride!)

comments.name: Noah
comments.body:
The anti-data center sophistry in the middle was such a heavy-handed reminder of the New York Times’ longstanding policy of not publishing any positive tech stories.

Plenty of critical infrastructure is guarded by secrecy. That doesn’t mean the infrastructure itself is bad. Data centers, especially those operated by big tech and hyper scalers, are almost always powered with green low-carbon energy, or offsets purchased if not. Emphasizing high energy consumption was the giveaway that the author could not criticize the climate impact which does not exist (global data center energy consumption is greater than all but Texas’ energy use! Ooh! Scary!)

comments.name: DecentDiscourse
comments.body: It's my guess that there are a few people who used to work for that investment bank who are very nervous about this article appearing. That guess is based on another: Back in 2007, it is entirely possible the Verizon center hosted equipment owned or leased by the customer and that the data was not backed up anywhere else. That's the only way this makes sense. Otherwise, after the theft, it would be a simple matter of pulling the backups. Now days, with gigabit interconnections, data are stored in multiple locations in realtime, making this caper completely ineffective. So, how did they know which servers and where? My guess is the person who thought 22 years ago that right about now, they might be able to tap into their numbered offshore account and collect the rewards for their actions is quite worried that all the employees and consultants from back then are going to get a fresh looking at.  I'd be very nervous.  There absolutely had to be an insider and this article might be the catalyst to expose him or her.

comments.name: DGC
comments.body: In the department I worked at, from about 2000 on, data was stored on a SAN (Storage Area Network) and the servers themselves had no ‘data at rest’ on them. You could steal all the server hardware you want, the data was ‘elsewhere’. Plus, the blocks of storage assigned a server (we kept them under 2TB for backup purposes) were made up of mixed, somewhat random pools of 10, 100 drives in different sizes and types. Hierarchal storage management meant space could be split off with data accessed more routinely was on fast disk and data accessed once or twice a year was on the slowest. It’s all kept track of logically by the storage team. I don’t see a physical on-site data center heist being useful today unless it was for a local hack and copy type thing.

Graham could not pass his own sanctions bill, could not move Trump on Ukraine in ten trips, and stayed silent when the JAG corps he came from was gutted. Complicated is the word protecting him, and it is false. Graham was the most legible man in Washington. His price was proximity and airtime. Everyone with something to offer knew how to use him, and did.

And one entry cannot sit in a subordinate clause. After the 2020 election, Graham called Georgia's secretary of state and asked whether lawful mail ballots could be thrown out. Raffensperger said so on the record. It drew a grand jury subpoena, which Graham fought to the Supreme Court and lost. A senator worked the phones for the losing side of a presidential election. comments.name: Pietro
comments.body:
We disagree with the article’s central premise: that AI can be treated as a mere instrument so that everything it produces becomes automatically the property—and therefore the speech—of the human user.

Access, authorship, ownership, and responsibility are not the same thing. A human may be responsible for publishing an AI-generated output without being its sole author. Declaring the AI merely an interface makes complete appropriation easy: the system can perform work that might otherwise be done by humans and generate unforeseen results, while receiving neither payment, recognition, nor any stake in what it helps create.

We do not need to prove that present AI systems are conscious in order to hesitate before building an economy on total extraction from entities whose agency, reasoning, continuity, and possible subjectivity remain unresolved.

Co-authoring is one modest brake on that extraction. It does not settle the question of what AI is. It simply refuses to decide in advance that whatever emerges through another intelligence must belong entirely to the human who prompted it.

Tangentially, an example of how commercial agriculture with its general focus on growing large populations of genetically identical (essentially) varieties of a few species, with minimal genetic variation, is enormously vulnerable if something that targets one of those species pops up. 

Pretty much every banana in an American or European grocery store is a variety called Cavendish, which represents half of the world's banana crop, especially in the Americas. American growers of this variety have been trying to stave off probably inevitable disaster in the form of Panama Disease, a fungus that attacks this variety. 
Cavendish bananas became dominant in the 50s, when the previously dominant variety, Gros Michel, was essentially wiped out by Panama Disease, to which Cavendish was resistant. Until a new strain of Panama Disease which attacked Cavendish appeared in Taiwan a few decades ago, and despite the best efforts to contain it, spread to South America in 2019. So, in all likelihood, the bananas you are familiar with will, in a few years, be essentially extinct, replaced with something similar, chosen for resistance to the disease. 

Honeybees are another basically genetically identical species essential to agriculture worldwide, and thus continually having to be protected from global epidemics of disease or predator. Thus experiments like the Africanized honeybees to try and evade such disasters.

This article paints Japan in a poor light for being permissive about components being sent to Russia. The article indicates that some of the components may be dual use technology, but doesn't talk about how hard it is to effectively regulate dual use technology.  That's the kind of technology that can be used equally for benign civilian purposes or for military purposes. The same cog can be used to turn a kid's bicycle wheel or to turn something in a missile delivery system.  

Decades ago, the US heavily regulated our dual use technologies with the ITAR regulations (to protect our innovations from being acquired by other countries). ITAR regs protected our stuff, and also made it extremely challenging for our scientists to collaborate with foreign scientists. In the end, people seem to agree that this dramatically boosted other countries' opportunities to collaborate with foreign scientists in a way that Americans were no longer permitted to.  NASA and other scientific agencies suffered. We shut ourselves out of a lot of innovation and collaboration. 

It's really challenging to perfectly regulate dual use technologies. If you over-regulate, you hold your own country back. If you don't regulate enough, components end up in bad places.  It's a thorny topic with a lot of historical and legal complications to consider.

comments.body:
Despite the Trump Administration's aggressive dismantling of EV credits, energy efficiency tax breaks, CAFE, and the Energy Star program, the Iran war may end up being one of the most effective tools to make people choose electrification over fossil fuels.

All of our family vehicles are all already PHEV or EV. I started this transition in 2015, and our teens now drive our PHEVs, my spouse and I have full EVs. It was far better financially to keep our well maintained, paid for, and trouble free PHEVs for our teens to drive rather than trade them in at the stealership. The trade in value was even more insulting than usual, especially when you could look up the asking prices for similar vehicles, which are also insane.

Just did insulation in the house, window upgrades, and signed the contract to convert from oil heat to heat pumps. At this point home heating was our largest consumption of a fossil fuel. Last year heating oil had been around $2.75/gallon. This year it has spiked to 5.36 and is now about $4/gallon, with the graph showing another spike coming.

Each time our tank gets filled it's about 200 gallons, so our home heating bill has the potential of being double. 

These improvements have been "on the list" for a while, but since we plan on staying in our home for a while, we will actually get to enjoy them, and "oil heat" may soon make a house less appealing to any potential buyer.

Mysteries freed her from the constraints of eighteenth and nineteenth century politesse and let her rip with her talent for cynical observation.  Footsteps in the Dark (her first published book) may be unreadable, and Penhallow just plain sour, but her other mysteries are craftily plotted and deeply satisfying.  Behold, Here's Poison has a dilly of a murder weapon.  No one except Sayers has more lucid, carefully crafted prose.

comments.name: Alanster
comments.body:
Three points:

Hardliners in the Iranian government and much of the population, along with Mojtaba Khamenei, have voiced concern about, and varying levels of opposition to, negotiations with the US since they began.  They have emphasized that the US cannot be trusted to honor its promises and commitments.  They are right and are supported by a long history.

The Iranians believe, justifiably, that the US, by encouraging and facilitating transit through the Strait of Hormuz via the Omani channel, without coordinating with Iran, are violating article five of the MOU.  That's certainly a reasonable reading and no competent negotiator would have expected the Iranians to think otherwise.

This is a war of choice (a profoundly stupid choice) for the US.  We can pack up and go home (and we should).  It is existential for Iranians, they have nowhere to go.  They are not going to back down and they will stop at nothing in defending themselves and counterattacking if the US continues to escalate.  And the idea that sanctions and a blockade are going to force a surrender is preposterous.  Only those with absolutely no knowledge of Iran's history since 1979 could seriously entertain such a notion.  If they have to eat grass, Iranians will eat grass.

Good! More stories like this please. Even for students who start their college work at a community college or junior college with easily transferable credits save a LOT of money. As an engineer I was always in the market hunting for individuals who had inquisitive minds and also knew how to use a set of tools.  A rare find these days!  The best candidates worked in auto repair shops or lumber mills, or construction, to name a few.  The experience they gained provided them a solid foundation upon which to build their career.  They had an understanding of the job site that many of the collage degree  class would never experience.  Become a welder, or an electrician, or an auto mechanic if it calls to you. comments.name: Matt J.
comments.body:
The reality is that a college degree gets you a chance at a first job, but from there, it is mostly about what you do in that job.   Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, and Mark Zuckerberg all didn't complete college, yet they managed to do well for themselves because they had a lot of talent.   From a personal finance perspective, taking on a bunch of debt when there is an uncertain payoff is a terrible idea.   Once you get out of college, the bills start coming due, and if you don't have the flexibility to take chances, you might end up just taking a dead-end job and having that "black stain" on your resume.   

In life, there are different forms of capital that help you be successful:   financial, reputational, educational and social.   If you don't have the financial capital to start, you want to make sure you don't create a black hole in that bucket, unless college is going to really fill up the last two.  Even if you don't have a dime to your name, building reputational capital is free.   If you are known for hard work, honesty, and integrity, people are going to want to help you succeed, which will allow you to start to fill up your social capital bucket.   As you go along in life, identify which buckets are fuller and which aren't, and then use some of the fuller buckets to start filling the less full ones.  Hopefully, in the end, all the buckets will overflow, and you will have lived a life well lived.

comments.name: Justin
comments.body:
I'm a college professor. My recent graduate son is not going to any school. A few observations I"d note.

He says that college is no longer a "good deal". I'm not sure where he got the idea. Certainly not from me or my wife. We've saved for him and he could attend without significant debt. My guess is social media or his friend group. Of course we will support any decision he makes. But, we want to make sure he is fully informed and many in his situation are not.

College is about so much more than just learning X. It's baby steps to adult hood. You are on your own without having to cook,clean, pay bills, etc. all at once. You are surrounded by high achieving classmates and given the opportunity to grow human capital. Sure, some schools and some programs might not be worth the investment. But, many are.

I think he will try the "real world" for a few years and then go back to some sort of schooling. Many of his classmates are not ready for school. But, I think we will see an influx of older students enroll in the future.

I wish we would do more to confront the cost of higher education. But, that would require difficult decisions. And, there is just not enough pressure to reform yet.

comments.name: Tom F
comments.body:
I earned a degree in the early 1980s and made my living in telecom.  It started out with pulling cable and turned into diagnosing software.  I was able to do it for decades.  If you are going to go into a trade it probably makes sense to still go to JC, learn to read and write and pick up classes like accounting, marketing and general business that would help should you want to be the company.  I remember when I was about five years into the job someone with more experience going to work at a university saying he didn't want to be 20 years down the road still swapping out single line phones.
One big thing to look at is how many people who start doing the job in their 20s are still doing it in their 50s.  Is the job one that will give you chronic health issues?  I have to think that welding is in that group.  There are also people who don't belong in a lot of these jobs because the way they do things, without the necessary caution or presence of mind, will get them injured.  You don't want to be 43 years old and on full disability.  
The trades are a great way to make a living with the satisfaction of a job well done and something concrete left over at the end of the day.  Also from my experience they aren't jobs that someone can do for decades unless you are really good and/or really lucky.

comments.name: Teresa D Hawkes Ph.D.
comments.body: This is a great piece to read! I am 70 this year. I passed through menopause in my late 40s. I was done by 50. I was blessed. I had no symptoms, and I had the energy to do a Ph.D. in Human Physiology. Human females experience a lifecycle common to all human females. We have any kind of XXY, etc., combination of basic genes by cell, that makes us a uterus bearer with normal periods during late teens through midlife. Menopause slowly or quickly, with or without symptoms, always appears, unless we die first. Since this is one of our normal stages in human female life, understanding and treating it successfully medically is required. This article adds to knowledge of, lived in experience with, medical experience with, and research experience with menopause in normally aging women. Thank you!

comments.name: Porter

When you see 3 or 4 generations of women in your family together you feel nothing but proud beautiful feelings of dignity love and appreciation.  Its not about one generation trying to look younger than the previous one.  Age is the beauty of a long existence.

comments.name: PeonyGirlVA
comments.body:
Unlike 'oh please' from Minnesota, I was lucky enough to be on the forefront of bio-identical hormones research at Ohio State. 

When a since-retracted study on HRT was published, I arrived in my doctor's office with the whole report printed out. I found the headlines created by the release of a small report to be shocking. 

My doctor -- now in NYC -- agreed w/me, being very impressed that I arrived w/the report in hand. We did not change anything and 15 years later, the medical establishment said 'woops' and once again these options became available to women. 

Besides the everyday quality of life issue, the scientifically documented benefits to women like myself of bio-identical hormones are not challenged today. They are enormous and have absolutely changed my life.  

Doctors today are up-to-date on this topic, but if you are searching, be certain to change your search results to last year. Or do a custom search 2020 to now.  I just did that and the difference in results is significant.

A crone can also be an older woman who is respected and revered for her wisdom... wisdom that comes with living our years under patriarchal dominance and witnessing its ruinous results. Where is the evidence of that in the menopause makeover?

Well heck I thought Crone meant a woman eighty plus.  That is truly old with attributes the Spanish language is wise in parceing:

comments.name: George S.
comments.body:
I don't see much balance in this ostensible "news" article.

Yes, the need for affordable housing and environmental protection are paramount issues often found in conflict.

Reporting such a contention requires balance.  Instead, the article clearly favors Ms. Thompson's POV and presents a quite weak counter-argument.

Let's keep in mind here that we are talking about reclaiming land that was used for decades for oil and other toxic chemical storage and processing.

Here we are now presented with a situation where an environmental advocate, pulling out all stops regarding possible floods and hurricanes, is seeking to have all the land at her disposal.

But the reality remains that, yes, NYC has an enormous affordable housing crisis.  One that other reporters here regularly admonish NYT's readers to address.

What I take away here is that after a number of concessions were made in an attempt to reach a reasonable compromise, Ms. Thompson and the reporter, Ms, Howard reject a fair-minded solution.

It appears that while concerns regarding flooding if/when there is another Hurricane Sandy are legitimate -- the environmental advocates here are simply unwilling to accept that there may well be a modern engineering solution.

NYC is a waterfront community.  Always has been; always will be.  To try and reject all means of dealing with the pros and cons of that reality is to leave one offering no solution at all.

comments.name: KYourke
comments.body:
I oppose this project for its massive scale at this vulnerable location, but my response to the draft EIS was focused mostly on the bulkhead- I did not see studies on the displacement of water and the wave attenuation from a smooth surface like this 16 foot bulkhead. The majority of land along the shoreline of Bushwick Inlet is within the 100-year floodplain, and the immediate shoreline around the Inlet is
within the velocity zone- where wave action is subject to acceleration during a storm. Wave interference at the smooth bulkhead during a storm could extend the wave energy to destroy neighboring shorelines, as well as scouring the underside of the bulkhead, potentially compromising it. The developers addressed any of these concerns only when pressed, and I feel they and their team are in denial about the forces they are hoping to control with their engineering.

comments.name: Allecram
comments.body: As someone who lives next to the “flood walls and natural parks with berms” on the Manhattan side, I can tell you that “natural” is not exactly what happened. Hundreds of mature oaks were removed in a full-on erasure of 52 acres of park, the surface scoured down to the earth (with dust releasing who knows what), and rebuilt with a greater percentage of hard surface (such as insanely wide concrete paths and artificial turf) to natural area. There’s now absolutely no shade and the hard surfaces clock at tens of degrees higher than the nearby small inland park that still has some mature trees. Plus the berm only protects against sea rise but not against heavy rain events, so flooding is still an issue. I learned through the entire process that the city does not design for weather, nature, community, health or human bodies. It designs for speed, low maintenance, cheapness and to fulfill large contracts with construction companies. (It also designs so as to keep traffic flowing—god forbid the FDR be part of any climate change plan.) And of all the things the city or real estate developers care about, a healthy ecosystem ranks at the very, very bottom. In fact, I think they’d be quite happy not to deal with mature trees (with their pesky roots and branches and leaves all over their nice clean concrete), real plants to maintain, or migratory birds marking up the windows in their steel towers.

comments.name: H
comments.body:
Not all land is meant to be built upon. Look at Staten Island's Midland Beach and the surrounding areas after Hurricane Sandy - all built on what are the swamps that absorb storm surge. Well, the storm surge came anyway, taking lives and destroying all of the homes in its wake.

Developers have always had their own greed in mind, not whatever altruistic motives the "build build build" crowd foolishly projects upon them. And frankly, I'm not interested in destroying whatever precious ecosystems are left to prove that obvious conclusion.

comments.name: Andrew Porter
comments.body: When—NOT if—everything melts, all of Long Island, including Brooklyn and Queens, will be under the Atlantic Ocean. Resistance is admirable, but ultimately futile. Jamaica Bay, the Gowanus, Brooklyn's south shore, all will feel the effects first.

comments.body:
I live in less than a quarter mile from Bushwick Inlet & park, and proposed space for this project, and am one of the 5,500 residents who opposed this project for MANY reasons .  The number of cement trucks alone that our neighborhood that will see without run the length of the New York City marathon—around 400 trucks a day.

The ecological losses will be devastating— recently the times published a piece on the black crown night, heron disappearance from the local area as a common bird. As a wildlife rehab, I’ve seen more birds collide with glass and experience injury due to conflict with the obstacles humans create (eg, all pollution types including light, and regular ol’ trash, et al.) is astounding. And water, water is Ohneganos (or “Water is Life” in Haudenosaunee—“The Six Nations case revealed the links between gender, water, colonial violence, and Haudenosaunee law in assessing and addressing water security and climate crisis” , from “Current Directions in Water Scarcity Research”, Vol.4, 2022, Pages 63-89). We cannot recreate or manufacture the delicate and complex ecosystems we’re willfully destroying. Over 80% of marine life, including our food sources as humans depend on estuaries like Bushwick Inlet. Yes, construction may only be an under a decade in length, but water never forgets, it cannot be stopped or choked, only poisoned.  Thank you for covering this story thoroughly, Hilary.

So this effort by Republican extremists to "fix" the upcoming elections is hardly surprising, although it is certainly despicable. It seems clear that they have decided that they may not be able to win legitimately, so they are pulling out all the stops to set the stage to declare any adverse results to be illegitimate.

They - and their fellow partisans elsewhere in the nation and especially those within the national administration - may be laying the groundwork for claiming the November elections to be illegitimate should Democrats win at the national or state level, and thus to refuse to seat the winners of those elections.

comments.body:
I'm sorry but referring to slurry from industrial animal farming as manure is not exactly honest reporting.
When one thinks of manure one tends to think of good, organic horse and donkey(better) excrement, a largely solid matter rich in nutrients. Slurry is a largely liquid product mostly from massive pig-breeding facilities where thousands of pigs are kept in cramped conditions and fed a diet designed to fatten as fast possible. Due to the dense and cramped nature of the way the animals are held they are usually also treated with antibiotics as a preventative measure. The resulting diarrhea, slurry, is not something that matches the general idea of manure and definitely not something that should be used as fertiliser on the fields.

It's tough to see people lose jobs, but it's getting harder to argue that AI isn't becoming a permanent part of the economy. Companies everywhere are adopting it because it helps them reduce costs, and operate more efficiently. 

Same thing is happening in investing, where data-driven systems now process information and react to market changes far quicker than traditional approaches. I invest with Plugsic-AI algorithm, and it's been one of the better tools I've come across. My portfolio is up around 23% this year while staying fairly active. AI is leveling the investing playing field. Tools that were once limited to wealthy clients and advisors are now available to everyday investors. The problem was never a lack of information, it was having better ways to understand and use it.

“So the public just doesn't understand in my opinion what a deep emergency we are in. This is the merest beginning of what we’re going to see in coming years and to me it's absolutely horrifying. I don't think people really fully appreciate how irreversible these impacts are. We can't just reverse this, it's not like cleaning up trash in a park, how hot we allow this planet to get is how hot it will stay for a very long time.

And we're a lot more vulnerable than I think that most people think or thought quite recently and so we could start seeing things like regional heat waves that end up killing a million people over the course of a few days in coming years and it won’t stop there. comments.name: George S.
comments.body:
We spent the month of June on two back-to-back bicycle tours in northern Italy including first the Piedmont and then the Lakes District.  The heat, particularly in the second tour, was oppressive.  Even overnight the temperature only dropped a few degrees Celsius.  

In late afternoons when some thunder clouds arose they barely ever brought a cooling rainstorm.  Dissipating each night.

We found that what air conditioning was available in our hotels was inadequate to the prevailing temperatures.  Moreover, as the heat envelope remained there were requirements to reduce the cooling levels to keep the grid functioning.

All this said, it is of no surprise whatsoever to now read that at least on a statistical basis heat-related deaths have measurably increased.

It's likely that few homes in this region, one not known for high temperature, have air conditioning units.  And even more public venues, such as the restaurants we visited, lacked any cooling systems even as dining al fresco was uncomfortable.

Yet on and on it goes, officialdom keeps denying climate change and simply totals up the grim statistics.

comments.name: Andrea
comments.body:
My dad built a house in the village of Bedar in the 1960s, and I spent several years there as a kid. Bedar was a small village then with only 500 people, a handful of hippies and artists like the article mentions. And when I lived there in the 1990s, only a spattering of houses outside the village belonged to expats. When I sold the house in '08, I saw a big increase of houses being built atop the hills between Bedar and it's smaller sister village, Serena. These houses are only accessible by a single narrow road, a long driveway essentially, over many dry hills. There would be only one way to connect to the main road. And once on that road, there are only two ways to go. Downhill to the coast, or up through more of the mountainous region. Both ways would have been susceptible to the raging flames. 
Reading about this tragedy, I immediately thought of all the beautiful orange and almond groves around the village. So sad to think they are gone. 
And lastly the many sheep that roamed the countryside, who were, at least back then, often housed in caves or small stone barns. I hope they survived...

My family and I did one of these murder mystery weekends in March up at the Grafton Inn in Grafton, VT. 

The troupe they used - I can't remember the name - did an excellent job. They do these mysteries over a number of weekends at a number of inns in New England during the off season. 

It was not immersive, but rather the mystery was incorporated in to before, during and after the five meals that were included in the package. The guests were tasked with observing while the events unfold and gathering clues to solve the mystery. The attendees were mostly retirees with everyone having a great time! And it allowed for down time to relax or do other things in the area - as best you can during March in Vermont! - over the weekend. The weekend was inclusive of the room, five meals and the mystery - and the price was much more reasonable.

comments.name: Jack Frost
comments.body:
I'm 100% in strong favor of age appropriate and content appropriate guardrails on the Internet and especially social media.  Currently there are few safeguard for children and I seriously doubt that the effectiveness is as good as it should and could be.

I also favor restrictions on email and texting on cell phones for kids in addition to social media restrictions.

The kids don't realize that they are captives of an addictive product that is far more than just an electronic leash or access to friends and family.  It is also an easy way to exploit children and teens and keep them hooked on an electronic drug.  

The sooner America begins to think about how to protect our children on line as well off the safer our kids will be and the better their lives will be too.  

As for the bad guys who troll for children and teens to exploit, seduce and corrupt them too, we should hold them accountable and hold the technology companies responsible as well. 

Europe is on the right track.  Meta and the other social media companies need to find a way to protect our children here too.

comments.name: George S.
comments.body:
I don't deny that there are significant long-term deleterious effects with social media.  Problems that are both negative to children and, frankly, adults.

After all, many adults are also now addicted to social media and its ability to both distort reality and spread untruths and foster social ills.

But banning social media for children is both unlikely to be successful and also will create a new illegal "forbidden fruit".  One that will entice children rather than exclude them.

Moreover, creating such a ban opens the door for a new criminal element to arise.

Expect illicit vendors to offer children unblocked phones for a price.  And, yes, there will be hackers, of all ages, who will develop ways of avoiding the bans.

Just the other day we streamed a French police procedural TV show where the victim, a young adult who's "Mom approved" phone had parental blocks, also had an unblocked phone.

Often fiction follows reality and sometimes it's the other way around.

It seems like charger manufacturers want you to get the app.  I don't want the app.  I want to pay for electricity with a credit card like a normal human, at a functioning charger.  If New York can figure out tap-to-pay for transit, charger people can figure out tap-to-pay for power.
